title: Test-Time Training Done Right
one_liner: Large Chunk Test-Time Training updates a model's fast weights on very large token chunks, which raises hardware utilization and allows much larger temporary state while the model is producing outputs.
lead: Test-time training updates a subset of model weights while the model is already processing a sequence. Those updated fast weights act as temporary memory for the current context. In earlier TTT systems, the updates happen on very small blocks such as 16 or 64 tokens (the small text pieces a model processes). That makes the update rule tightly sequential and wastes modern GPU hardware because each update is too small to use the machine well. It also limits the size of the nonlinear state, since a tiny update budget cannot maintain a large temporary memory. This paper moves in the opposite direction. Large Chunk Test-Time Training, or LaCT, updates fast weights over chunks from thousands to millions of tokens. That makes each update large enough for high hardware utilization and large enough to support a much bigger temporary state. The result is better long-context handling across text, image sets, and video because the online memory update becomes both scalable and practical.

problem.h2: Why small online updates waste both memory capacity and hardware
paras: In test-time training, a model processes incoming data and updates a small set of fast weights while it reads that same sequence. Those fast weights store context-dependent information that ordinary fixed weights cannot memorize for the current example.

Earlier methods update those weights every few tokens. That seems natural if you want fine-grained causality, but it creates two bottlenecks. First, each update is too small for a GPU to process efficiently, so most of the hardware stays idle during the fast-weight step. Second, very small updates force the online state to stay small, since a larger nonlinear memory would make each update too costly.

The paper argues that this design choice is not fundamental. Many tasks can tolerate chunk-level updates instead of tiny block updates. Once the chunk becomes large, the online optimization step turns into a dense computation that current hardware can execute well, and the temporary state can scale up with it.

callout.html: Replace tiny frequent fast-weight updates with much larger chunk updates, then use the larger update budget to maintain a larger temporary memory state.

paras: The paper changes the granularity of test-time weight updates. Standard TTT treats the update step as a tiny online loop. LaCT turns it into a large batched update that better matches the way current accelerators execute large table-of-numbers multiplications, because those devices deliver more throughput when one update contains enough parallel work.

hidden.name: How much temporary information the fast weights can store
paras: A test-time training layer is only useful if its fast weights can hold enough information from earlier context to help predict later content, because later predictions improve only when the temporary state preserves details the fixed model would otherwise forget. If the temporary state is too small, it cannot preserve much beyond local patterns. If the state is large but each update is tiny, then updating that state becomes too slow.

So the hidden quantity is state capacity under a fixed compute budget. LaCT improves this quantity by making each update much larger, which gives the optimizer enough work to support a larger temporary state without collapsing hardware utilization.

heat.caption: Darker cells highlight the ingredients that raise usable temporary memory. Low-value cells show the small-update regime that wastes capacity.

reads.html: The real question is not whether fast weights exist, but whether they can store enough context without making each update too slow to run.

Large chunk updates improve hardware utilization and permit much larger nonlinear state, so the TTT layer can act as a higher-capacity temporary memory over very long contexts because each update now spans enough data to justify the cost of maintaining that larger state.

mechanism.h2: Why larger chunks improve both throughput and memory
paras: Modern accelerators favor large dense workloads. A tiny fast-weight update touches too little data per launch, so compute units wait on overhead and memory movement. When the update covers thousands of tokens instead, the same algorithm becomes a larger table-of-numbers multiplication that the hardware can execute much more fully.

The bigger chunk also changes what state sizes are practical. With tiny updates, a large nonlinear state would make the online step too expensive at every block. With chunked updates, the cost is amortized over many more tokens, so the system can afford a larger temporary state per update.

This matters beyond text because small-block causality is awkward for unordered or grid-like data such as image sets or video token grids. Chunk updates relax that assumption. The model can adapt over a broad context window instead of pretending the data is best handled as a long chain of tiny blocks.

stages.s: Long context chunk from text, images, or video
Accumulate a large batch for online update
Run dense fast-weight optimization on the chunk
Store more context in a larger temporary state
Use the updated state on later chunks
Higher throughput and stronger long-context behavior because each update uses the hardware more fully and carries a larger temporary state

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose an older method updates every 32 tokens, while LaCT updates every 2048 tokens.
The LaCT update uses 64 times more tokens per optimization step.
That gives the update access to much more context and turns many tiny launches into one large dense computation.
If the larger step keeps the temporary memory useful over the whole chunk, the model gains both throughput and context capacity.

math.note: The main change is not the update rule itself. It is choosing a chunk size large enough that the online update becomes hardware-friendly and can support a larger temporary state.

items.b: Chunk size is too large for the task.
items.html: If the task truly depends on very fine-grained causal updates, waiting for a huge chunk before adapting may delay useful memory formation.

A very large chunk improves utilization only if the device can still store the intermediate layer outputs and fast-weight optimizer state required for that chunk, because the larger batch is helpful only when it fits in memory without forcing expensive fallback behavior.
A higher-capacity temporary state can store more context, but it can also overfit a chunk if the online optimizer or learning rate is poorly controlled.
Choose the largest chunk that still fits device memory and still matches the task's temporal structure, then tune the online optimizer so the temporary state captures context without drifting.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a long-sequence task such as language modeling or multi-view reconstruction. Implement two TTT layers with the same base architecture: one that updates fast weights every 32 or 64 tokens, and one that updates once per chunk of 2048 or more tokens. Measure hardware utilization, temporary state size, throughput, and task score as context length increases.
demo.closing: The demo should show that larger chunk updates help not only because there are fewer optimizer calls, but because each call is large enough to exploit the hardware and to maintain a richer temporary memory.
